appraisal_events.evidence: « seul Swann ne s'était pas déridé » ; « il n'était pas très content que Cottard fît rire de lui devant Forcheville » ; « le peintre, au lieu de répondre d'une façon intéressante à Swann, ce qu'il eût probablement fait s'il eût été seul avec lui, préféra se faire admirer des convives ».
appraisal_events.explanation: Swann is left outside the table's collective laughter, mocked in front of his rival Forcheville, and then passed over by the painter, who deliberately trades a real answer to Swann for the applause of the assembled guests. The narrator explicitly notes that Swann would have received an interesting reply in private, which frames the choice as a deliberate slighting of him before the group.

appraisal_events.evidence: « — Et un font douze, s'écria trop tard le docteur dont personne ne comprit l'interruption. »
appraisal_events.explanation: Cottard's pun arrives mistimed and lands on an uncomprehending table, so the narrator stages his second bid for wit as a plain social failure, in contrast with the joke at Swann's expense that had just succeeded.

status_effects.explanation: Swann is singled out as the only guest not sharing the table's amusement and is then set aside by the painter in favour of the assembled convives, leaving him locally outside the group.

The painter takes and holds the floor with a prepared set piece on the dead master and wins the room's admiration, even though the narrator's framing treats the performance as vanity rather than substance.
His ill-timed and unintelligible pun falls flat before the same audience he had just amused, lowering him locally.

ambiguities: « le peintre » is the Verdurin-era designation of the figure later revealed as Elstir; the reference sheet deliberately keeps the name-view entity separate, so the annotation uses « le peintre » rather than resolving the identification.

The narrator both reports the painter's success with the guests and undercuts it (« préféra se faire admirer », the falsetto-singer simile, the crude enumeration ending « avec du caca »); reading the framing as ironized rather than neutral would cancel his positive rhetorical movement.
